name: GHK-Cu
lead: GHK-Cu is the copper(II) complex of the tripeptide glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine (GHK). The tripeptide binds copper strongly, was first isolated from human plasma, and is also found in saliva and urine [1]. In cosmetics it is listed as copper tripeptide-1 and appears in anti-aging, firming and hair-care products [1][2].

Plasma GHK is reported to average about 200 ng/ml at age 20 and about 80 ng/ml by age 60, a decline that is often cited by proponents [1][3]. Laboratory and animal studies describe stimulation of collagen and glycosaminoglycan synthesis, wound-healing effects, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity and changes in the expression of many genes [1][4]. Human evidence for appearance outcomes is limited to small topical studies; Wikipedia describes controlled facial studies of anti-wrinkle and firming activity as small and short, with further research needed [1].

Besides cosmetic creams, GHK-Cu is sold as a research peptide for injection, sometimes in blends with BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV that users call stacks. Sports medicine reviews describe such unapproved peptides as part of a gray market operating largely outside regulatory oversight [5][6]. The US FDA lists injectable GHK-Cu among bulk drug substances nominated for compounding and later withdrawn, and states that compounded injectable drugs containing it may pose a risk of immunogenicity, with limited human data available [7].

paras: GHK-Cu is widely used in anti-aging and hair-loss-prevention cosmetics [1]. A retail copper peptide facial serum listed on DailyMed is labelled to repair, tighten and address signs of premature aging, with external-use-only warnings [8]. Reviews discuss GHK as a topical anti-wrinkle peptide and note problems, including that GHK-Cu is hydrophilic and has limited permeation through the stratum corneum, which has motivated liposomal formulations [2][9]. A palmitoylated derivative (Pal-GHK) is also used in cosmetics [2].

GHK-Cu is not an approved drug. It is studied for wound healing and tissue repair. A registered phase 2 trial of topical GHK-Cu gel for acute skin wounds (punch biopsy wounds, 60 participants) began recruiting in 2026 [10]. A randomized trial examined copper tripeptide skin care products after CO2 laser resurfacing [11].

A 2025 review of topically applied GHK as an anti-wrinkle peptide describes the peptide's capacity for tissue regeneration and its promotion of collagen and glycosaminoglycan synthesis, while discussing advantages, problems and prospects [2]. The randomized trial in laser-resurfaced skin compared post-treatment regimens with and without GHK-Cu and assessed erythema over the recovery period [11]. A 2018 review concludes that GHK has multiple actions that it characterizes as health positive in light of gene-expression data [4].

Most mechanistic findings come from cell cultures and animals, such as stimulation of collagen synthesis by fibroblasts at picomolar to nanomolar concentrations, and improved wound healing in rabbits, rats, mice and pigs [1][12][13]. Orthopaedic and sports medicine reviews list GHK-Cu among wound-healing peptides but frame the human evidence for injectable use as limited [5][6][14].

Topical cosmetic products carry general warnings such as external use only and avoiding eyes [8]. The FDA states that compounded injectable GHK-Cu may pose a risk of immunogenicity because of aggregation and peptide-related impurities, and that human data to inform safety are limited [7]. Sports medicine reviewers describe gray-market peptides as operating outside regulatory oversight, with variable product quality [6].

A T Nation poster who used a blend containing GHK-Cu suggested it might be pulling copper into the skin and linked it to low copper or iron absorption, citing online reports from others; no study in the sources reviewed tests that claim [15].

GHK has a very high affinity for copper. In the complex, copper(II) is coordinated by nitrogens from the histidine imidazole and the glycine alpha-amino group, among others [1]. It is proposed that GHK may be released from collagen by proteases after injury as a signal of tissue damage, since the GHK sequence is present in the alpha-2 chain of type I collagen [1][13]. Proposed actions include attracting repair cells, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects, stimulating collagen, decorin and glycosaminoglycans, promoting blood vessel growth and altering the expression of large numbers of genes [1][12][4]. A 2012 review also discusses implications for oxidative stress and cognitive aging [16].

Loren Pickart (1938 to 2023) isolated GHK-Cu from human plasma albumin in 1973, after observing that liver cells from older donors behaved more like young cells when incubated in younger donors' blood; the active factor was identified as the tripeptide, and in 1977 the growth-modulating peptide was shown to be glycyl-histidyl-lysine [1]. In the late 1980s it attracted attention as a wound-healing agent, with studies showing stimulated collagen synthesis in fibroblasts and increased glycosaminoglycan and protein accumulation in rat wounds [1][13].

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: On T Nation, GHK-Cu appears mostly as one component of multi-peptide blends. Users describe a product they call KLOW (KPV, BPC-157, TB-500 and GHK-Cu) taken daily for joints and soft tissue, with GHK-Cu described as the skin and hair component; others ask about a similar GLOW stack for post-surgery recovery, or list GHK-Cu among compounds in their cycles for skin and looks [17][18][19][20][21]. One poster says they inject a peptide mix including GHK-Cu into a bursa [22].

Published human work on GHK-Cu is small. It includes a randomized trial of copper tripeptide skin care after CO2 laser resurfacing [11] and short controlled facial studies summarized in reviews [1][2]. Registered studies include a phase 2 topical gel trial in acute wounds, a planned study of a patch and circulating GHK and GHK-Cu levels in 100 healthy adults, an early-phase study of systemic and topical interventions using aging clocks, and a Hydrafacial skin-quality trial [10][23][24][25]. Studies of injectable peptide therapy in sports medicine are primarily reviews of preclinical and limited human evidence [5][6][14].

timeline.event: Loren Pickart isolates GHK-Cu from human plasma albumin [1].
The growth-modulating peptide is shown to be glycyl-histidyl-lysine [1].
GHK-Cu attracts attention as a wound-healing agent in animal and cell studies [1].
Randomized trial of copper tripeptide skin care after CO2 laser resurfacing is published [11].

lore.intro: GHK-Cu is discussed on T Nation chiefly as part of injectable peptide blends and as a skin and hair add-on to cycles [17][21].

claims.claim: GHK-Cu in a peptide blend supports skin and hair as well as injury recovery
claims.believers: A poster says the GHK-Cu in a KLOW blend is the skin and hair component, while the other peptides address soft tissue and inflammation, and another describes using it daily for years of injuries [17][19].
claims.experts: Reviews describe collagen and gene-expression effects mainly from cell and animal work, with human cosmetic studies small; sports medicine reviews call evidence for injectable peptides limited [1][5][14].

claims.claim: GHK-Cu is a 'looksmax' peptide that improves skin and appearance
claims.believers: A poster planning a cycle lists GHK-Cu among peptides for skin and tan and 'to look better' [21].
claims.experts: Controlled studies of topical GHK-Cu are small and short [1]; no published trial tests injectable GHK-Cu for appearance in the sources reviewed.

claims.claim: GHK-Cu can deplete copper or cause problems when taken in blends
claims.believers: One poster suspects a GHK-Cu blend was pulling copper into the skin and causing low iron-related problems, citing online reports [15].
claims.experts: No study in the sources reviewed tests this; the FDA instead cites immunogenicity risks for compounded injectables [7].

claims.claim: Injectable GHK-Cu is safe because it is a natural human peptide
claims.believers: Posters describe it as a naturally occurring peptide and use it routinely in stacks [17][19].
claims.experts: The FDA says compounded injectable GHK-Cu may pose a risk of immunogenicity through aggregation and impurities, with limited human data [7]; reviewers note gray-market quality variability [6].

claims.claim: GHK-Cu gives scar reduction and anti-aging
claims.believers: An older T Nation post links to a scar-reduction site promoting copper peptides for scar removal [26].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports animal wound-healing data and small human facial studies, with definitive conclusions awaiting more research [1].
